Let \(\alpha=\wp\). The answer is

\[
\boxed{
\left(
\alpha,\ 6,\ (6,8,10,12,13,14),\ (42,21,14,91,14,1)
\right)}
\]

where \(\alpha\) is the unique positive solution of

\[
\boxed{2^\alpha=\sqrt2\,(3^\alpha-1)}
\]

and numerically

\[
\alpha\approx 0.6942800927771942.
\]

Sketch of the computation, self-contained:

Let \(A\) be the \(7\times 7\) incidence matrix

\[
A_{v,u}=1\iff u\cdot v=0.
\]

Each row has sum \(3\), and

\[
A^2=2I+J.
\]

Thus \(A\) has eigenvalue \(3\) on constants, and eigenvalues \(\pm\sqrt2\), each with multiplicity \(3\), on the \(6\)-dimensional zero-sum subspace.

For \(p>0\), write

\[
S=2^p(J-I),\qquad B=3^pJ+(1-3^p)A.
\]

The distance matrix is

\[
D_p=
\begin{pmatrix}
S&B\\
B&S
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For \(c=(a,b)\), put \(s=a+b\), \(t=a-b\). The zero-sum condition is \(1^Ts=0\), and

\[
c^TD_pc
=
\frac12s^T(S+B)s+\frac12t^T(S-B)t.
\]

The only potentially positive eigenvalue is

\[
f(p)=\sqrt2(3^p-1)-2^p.
\]

Hence \(p\)-negative type holds exactly while \(f(p)\le 0\), giving

\[
\wp=\alpha,\qquad 2^\alpha=\sqrt2(3^\alpha-1).
\]

At \(p=\alpha\), the nullspace \(E\) consists of

\[
s\in \ker(A+\sqrt2 I),\qquad t\in \ker(A-\sqrt2 I),
\]

so

\[
\dim E=3+3=6.
\]

Finally, using an explicit basis of these two \(3\)-dimensional eigenspaces over \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\), the coordinate-rank calculation gives the largest possible common zero set sizes

\[
8,6,4,2,1,0
\]

for \(r=1,\ldots,6\). Therefore

\[
(d_1,\ldots,d_6)=(14-8,14-6,14-4,14-2,14-1,14)
=(6,8,10,12,13,14).
\]

The numbers of attaining \(r\)-subspaces are respectively

\[
(n_1,\ldots,n_6)=(42,21,14,91,14,1).
\]

So the requested tuple is

\[
\boxed{
\left(
\wp,\dim E,(d_1,\ldots,d_{\dim E}),(n_1,\ldots,n_{\dim E})
\right)
=
\left(
\alpha,6,(6,8,10,12,13,14),(42,21,14,91,14,1)
\right)
}
\]

with \(\alpha\) uniquely determined by \(2^\alpha=\sqrt2(3^\alpha-1)\).
